topics.title: Regular verbs in the present tense
topics.titleEn: Regular verbs in the present tense
topics.summary: The present-tense endings -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en, plus the spelling rules for stems in -d/-t and -z/-s/-ß.

explanation.heading: The endings
explanation.text: A regular verb takes the stem plus -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en for ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie.

explanation.heading: Two spelling rules
explanation.text: Verbs ending in -d or -t add an extra -e before the ending (arbeiten → du arbeitest). Verbs ending in -z, -s or -ß lose the -s of the du-ending (heißen → du heißt).

rules: kommen: ich komme, du kommst, er/sie/es kommt, wir kommen, ihr kommt, sie/Sie kommen.
Verbs ending in -d, -t insert -e: arbeiten → du arbeitest, er arbeitet, ihr arbeitet.
Verbs ending in -z, -s, -ß: the du-form ends in -t only: heißen → du heißt.
sein is irregular: ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind.

examples.de: ich komme
du kommst
arbeitest
examples.note: du-form; the stem ends in -t, so -est

examples.de: heißt
examples.note: du-form; the stem ends in -ß, so just -t

examples.de: bin
sind

exercises.prompt: Complete the du-form of kommen.
exercises.text: Woher ___ du?
exercises.explain: Regular du-ending is -st: du kommst.

exercises.prompt: arbeiten ends in -t, so the du-form takes an extra -e.
exercises.text: Wo ___ du?
exercises.explain: Verbs ending in -d or -t insert -e: du arbeitest.

exercises.prompt: heißen ends in -ß. Which du-form is right?
exercises.text: Wie ___ du?
exercises.explain: After -z, -s, -ß the du-ending is just -t.

exercises.prompt: Which form of sein goes with ihr?
exercises.text: ___ ihr aus Berlin?
exercises.explain: sein: ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind.

exercises.prompt: The ending is wrong. Correct the sentence.
exercises.text: Du wohnt in Tübingen.
exercises.explain: The du-form takes -st: du wohnst.

topics.title: Present: verbs with a separable prefix
topics.titleEn: Present tense: verbs with a separable prefix
topics.summary: The prefix leaves the verb and goes to the end of the sentence.

explanation.heading: The bracket
explanation.text: In a main clause the conjugated verb stands in position 2 and the separable prefix goes right to the end of the sentence. Together they frame everything in between.

rules: anrufen → Ich rufe dich an.
aufstehen → Wann stehst du auf?
The prefix carries the stress: ANrufen, AUFstehen.
In a question the verb still takes position 2 (W-question) or 1 (yes/no question); the prefix still goes last.

examples.de: Ich rufe dich an.
Wann stehst du auf?
Wir probieren das Lauftraining aus
Ihr kommt zum Leonardo-Campus-Run mit.
Annika und Tobias machen beim Lauftraining mit.

exercises.prompt: anrufen — where does the prefix go?
exercises.text: Ich rufe dich ___.
exercises.explain: The separable prefix goes to the end of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Put the sentence in the right order.
exercises.explain: W-word, verb in position 2, subject, prefix at the end.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: Ihr kommt mit zum Leonardo-Campus-Run auf.
exercises.explain: The prefix separates and goes last.

exercises.prompt: The prefix has not separated. Correct the sentence.
exercises.text: Annika und Tobias mitmachen beim Lauftraining.
answers: Annika und Tobias machen beim Lauftraining mit.
exercises.explain: In the present tense the prefix separates and goes to the end.

topics.title: Present: verbs with a separable prefix and modal verbs
topics.titleEn: Separable verbs together with a modal verb
topics.summary: With a modal verb the separable verb stays whole, in the infinitive, at the end.

explanation.heading: No separation
explanation.text: When a modal verb is present, it takes position 2 and the separable verb goes to the end of the sentence as a whole infinitive — the prefix does not come off.

rules: Modal verb in position 2, separable infinitive at the end, written as one word.
mitmachen → Ich möchte unbedingt beim Lauftraining mitmachen.
mitnehmen → Tim kann uns im Auto mitnehmen.

examples.de: Ich möchte unbedingt beim Lauftraining mitmachen.
Tim kann uns im Auto mitnehmen.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: Tim kann uns im Auto mitnehmen.
Tim kann uns im Auto nehmen mit.
Tim mitkann uns im Auto nehmen.
Tim nimmt uns im Auto mitkann.
answers: Tim kann uns im Auto mitnehmen.
exercises.explain: With a modal verb the separable verb stays whole at the end.

exercises.prompt: Add the modal verb möchte.
exercises.from: Ich mache beim Lauftraining mit.
answers: Ich möchte unbedingt beim Lauftraining mitmachen.
exercises.explain: The prefix rejoins the verb, which goes to the end as an infinitive.

exercises.prompt: The separable verb should not be split here. Correct it.
exercises.text: Ich möchte beim Lauftraining machen mit.
exercises.explain: With a modal verb the infinitive stays in one piece.

exercises.prompt: Order the sentence.
answers: Tim kann uns im Auto mitnehmen.
exercises.explain: Subject, modal verb, middle field, infinitive last.

topics.title: Present: verbs with a stem-vowel change
topics.titleEn: Present tense: verbs with a stem-vowel change
topics.summary: In the du- and er/sie/es-forms some verbs change e→ie/i or a→ä, au→äu.

explanation.heading: Where the change happens
explanation.text: The vowel changes only in the du-form and the er/sie/es-form. The other four forms keep the plain stem.

rules: e → ie: lesen → du liest, er liest.
e → i: sprechen → du sprichst, er spricht; treffen → du triffst, er trifft.
a → ä: fahren → du fährst, er fährt; schlafen → du schläfst, er schläft.
au → äu: laufen → du läufst, er läuft.
wissen is special: ich weiß, du weißt, er weiß.
wir, ihr and sie/Sie never change the vowel: wir lesen, ihr lest, sie lesen.

examples.de: du liest
er/sie/es lie st
sprichst
fährst
läufst
weiß

exercises.prompt: fahren, er-form.
exercises.text: Er ___ jeden Tag mit dem Rad.
exercises.explain: a → ä in the du- and er-forms: du fährst, er fährt.

exercises.prompt: sprechen, du-form.
exercises.text: ___ du Deutsch?
exercises.explain: e → i: du sprichst.

exercises.prompt: Which form is correct?
exercises.text: Ihr ___ ein Buch.
exercises.explain: The ihr-form keeps the plain stem: ihr lest.

exercises.prompt: laufen, er-form?
exercises.text: Er ___ sehr schnell.
exercises.explain: au → äu: du läufst, er läuft.

exercises.prompt: The vowel should not change here. Correct the sentence.
exercises.text: Wir fähren nach Berlin.
exercises.explain: Only du and er/sie/es change the vowel.

topics.title: Use of the present tense
topics.summary: The present also expresses the future, and haben/sein prefer the preterite over the perfect.

explanation.heading: Present for the future
explanation.text: German uses the present tense plus a time expression pointing forward to talk about the future — no special future form is needed.

explanation.heading: haben and sein
explanation.text: For haben and sein German mainly uses the preterite rather than the perfect.

rules: Present + a future time expression = future: Morgen gehe ich ins Zentrum Paul Klee.
For haben and sein use mainly the preterite instead of the perfect.
sitzen takes haben in the perfect, but in southern Germany and Switzerland sein is used.

examples.de: Morgen gehe ich ins Zentrum Paul Klee.
For haben and sein use mainly preterite instead of perfect!
sitzen : use haben for the perfect tense, but in south Germany and CH use sein .
examples.note: a regional difference the document points out

exercises.prompt: How does German usually express this future plan?
exercises.text: ___ ich ins Zentrum Paul Klee.
exercises.explain: The present tense plus a future time expression is the normal way.

exercises.prompt: Which region uses sein in the perfect of sitzen?
exercises.explain: The document notes that sitzen takes haben, but south Germany and CH use sein.

exercises.prompt: For haben and sein, which past tense does German mainly use?
exercises.explain: haben and sein mainly appear in the preterite: ich hatte, ich war.

exercises.prompt: Use the preterite of sein.
exercises.text: Gestern ___ ich in Bern.
exercises.explain: For sein the preterite is preferred over the perfect.

topics.title: Perfect: irregular and mixed verbs
topics.titleEn: Perfect tense: irregular and mixed verbs
topics.summary: Irregular participles end in -en, mixed ones in -t with a vowel change.

explanation.heading: Two groups
explanation.text: Irregular verbs form the participle with ge- + (often changed) stem + -en. Mixed verbs combine an irregular stem change with the regular ending -t.

rules: Irregular: ge- + stem + -en — getroffen, gefunden, geschlafen, gelesen, geholfen, gesprochen.
Movement verbs take sein: ist gefahren, ist gekommen, ist gegangen, ist gelaufen.
Mixed: irregular stem + -t — gewusst, gedacht.
sein itself: ich bin gewesen, du bist gewesen, wir sind gewesen.

examples.de: ich habe getroffen
bin gefahren
habe gewusst
haben gedacht
bin gewesen

exercises.prompt: Which is the participle of denken?
exercises.text: Ich habe an dich ___.
exercises.explain: denken is a mixed verb: vowel change plus the regular -t.

exercises.prompt: Which auxiliary goes with gehen?
exercises.text: Wir ___ gegangen.
exercises.explain: Verbs of movement take sein.

exercises.prompt: Form the participle of schlafen.
exercises.text: Er hat gut ___.
exercises.explain: Irregular verbs end in -en: geschlafen.

exercises.prompt: The perfect of sein.
exercises.text: Ich bin in Berlin ___.
exercises.explain: sein → gewesen, with sein as the auxiliary.

exercises.prompt: The participle ending is wrong for this irregular verb. Correct it.
exercises.text: Wir haben das Buch gelest.
exercises.explain: lesen is irregular, so the participle ends in -en: gelesen.

topics.title: Perfect: regular verbs
topics.summary: ge-…-(e)t with haben or sein; verbs in -ieren take no ge-.

explanation.heading: The participle
explanation.text: A regular past participle is ge- + stem + -(e)t. Verbs ending in -ieren take no ge-: trainieren → trainiert.

explanation.heading: haben or sein
explanation.text: Most verbs form the perfect with haben. Verbs of movement or change of state take sein: starten → ist gestartet, passieren → ist passiert.

rules: Regular participle: ge- + stem + -t (schaffen → geschafft).
Stems in -t or -d add -et: starten → gestartet.
Verbs in -ieren take no ge-: trainieren → trainiert.
haben for most verbs; sein for movement and change of state: ist gestartet, ist passiert.

examples.de: ich habe geschafft
bin gestartet
habe trainiert
ist passiert

exercises.prompt: Form the participle of schaffen (regular).
exercises.text: Ich habe es ___.
exercises.explain: ge- + stem + -t.

exercises.prompt: trainieren ends in -ieren. Which participle is right?
exercises.text: Ich habe gestern ___.
exercises.explain: Verbs in -ieren form the participle without ge-.

exercises.prompt: Which auxiliary goes with starten?
exercises.text: Ich ___ gestartet.
exercises.explain: Verbs of movement or change of state take sein.

exercises.prompt: The stem ends in -t, so an -e is inserted.
exercises.text: Es ist etwas ___.
exercises.explain: passieren is an -ieren verb taking sein: ist passiert.

exercises.prompt: This -ieren verb should not take ge-. Correct it.
exercises.text: Wir haben zwei Stunden getrainiert.
exercises.explain: No ge- on verbs ending in -ieren.

topics.title: Perfect: verbs with inseparable prefixes (e.g. er-, be-, ver-, hinter-)
topics.titleEn: Perfect tense: verbs with inseparable prefixes
topics.summary: Verbs with er-, be-, ver-, hinter- form the participle without ge-.

explanation.heading: No ge-
explanation.text: Verbs whose prefix cannot separate — er-, be-, ver-, hinter- and others — take no ge- in the participle. The prefix is unstressed.

rules: ver- → vergessen; er- → erreicht; hinter- → hinterlassen; be- → besucht.
No ge- at all, and the participle still stands at the end of the sentence.
Whether the ending is -t or -en still depends on whether the verb is regular or irregular.

examples.de: Ich habe euch nicht vergessen .
Du hast den Hausmeister nicht erreicht.
Er hat keine Notiz hinterlassen .
Wir haben unsere Eltern besucht.

exercises.prompt: Form the participle of besuchen.
exercises.text: Wir haben unsere Eltern ___.
exercises.explain: Inseparable prefixes take no ge-: besucht.

exercises.prompt: Which participle is correct?
exercises.text: Ich habe euch nicht ___.
exercises.explain: ver- is inseparable, so no ge-.

exercises.prompt: Which prefix takes ge- in the participle?
exercises.explain: an- is separable (angerufen); be-, ver- and er- are inseparable and take no ge-.

exercises.prompt: This inseparable verb should not take ge-. Correct it.
exercises.text: Du hast den Hausmeister nicht geerreicht.
answers: Du hast den Hausmeister nicht erreicht.
exercises.explain: er- is inseparable, so the participle is erreicht.

topics.source: DaF kompakt neu A1–B1 — Grammar explanations

topics.title: Perfect: verbs with separable prefixes (e.g. an-, aus-, auf-, mit-, weg-, runter-,vorbei-, zurück-)
topics.titleEn: Perfect tense: verbs with separable prefixes
topics.summary: The ge- sits between the prefix and the stem: angerufen, aufgestanden.

explanation.heading: Where ge- goes
explanation.text: With a separable prefix the ge- of the participle is placed between the prefix and the stem, and the whole participle stands at the end of the sentence.

rules: prefix + ge + stem: an|ge|rufen, zurück|ge|rufen, aus|ge|füllt, mit|ge|nommen, runter|ge|bracht, weg|ge|fahren, auf|ge|standen.
The auxiliary stands in position 2, the participle at the end.
Movement verbs still take sein: sind weggefahren, bin aufgestanden.

examples.de: Ich habe dich heute mehrmals angerufen.
Du hast leider nicht zurückgerufen.
Er hat den Antrag vom Studierendenwohnheim ausgefüllt.
Sie sind heute Morgen weggefahren.
Am Sonntag bin ich erst um 11.00 Uhr aufgestanden.

exercises.prompt: Form the participle of anrufen.
exercises.text: Ich habe dich heute mehrmals ___.
exercises.explain: The ge- goes between prefix and stem: an-ge-rufen.

exercises.prompt: Which participle is correct?
exercises.text: Er hat den Antrag ___.
exercises.explain: aus + ge + füllt.

exercises.prompt: Which auxiliary goes with aufstehen?
exercises.text: Ich ___ um 11.00 Uhr aufgestanden.
exercises.explain: aufstehen is a change-of-state verb, so it takes sein.

exercises.prompt: The ge- is in the wrong place. Correct it.
exercises.text: Wir haben Leon nach Frankfurt genommen mit.
answers: Wir haben Leon nach Frankfurt mitgenommen.
exercises.explain: The participle is one word with ge- in the middle: mitgenommen.

topics.title: Imperative sentences
topics.summary: Three forms — du, ihr and Sie — built from the present tense.

explanation.heading: From the present tense
explanation.text: The du-imperative drops the -st ending and the pronoun. The ihr-imperative is simply the ihr-form without the pronoun. The Sie-imperative keeps the verb and puts Sie after it.

explanation.heading: Verbs with a vowel change
explanation.text: Verbs that change e → ie/i keep that change in the du-imperative (lies!), but verbs that change a → ä lose the umlaut (fahr!).

rules: du: drop -st and the pronoun — du kommst → Komm!
Stems in -d, -t and some others add -e: du redest → Rede!, du wartest → Warte!
ihr: the plain ihr-form — ihr kommt → Kommt!
Sie: verb first, then Sie — Sie kommen → Kommen Sie!
e → ie/i is kept: du liest → Lies!  a → ä is dropped: du fährst → Fahr!
Separable verbs split: du passt auf → Pass auf!
haben and sein are irregular: Hab keine Angst! / Sei vorsichtig! / Seien Sie vorsichtig!

examples.de: du kommst →Komm!
ihr kommt → Kommt!
Sie kommen → Kommen Sie!
du wartest → Warte!
du liest → Lies!
du fährst → F ahr!
du passt auf → Pass auf!
du bist → Sei vorsichtig!

exercises.prompt: du-imperative of kommen.
exercises.text: ___! Wir warten auf dich.
exercises.explain: Drop the -st and the pronoun: Komm!

exercises.prompt: fahren changes a → ä. Which du-imperative is right?
exercises.text: ___ bitte langsamer!
exercises.explain: The a → ä change is dropped in the imperative: Fahr!

exercises.prompt: lesen changes e → ie. Which du-imperative is right?
exercises.text: ___ den Text noch einmal!
exercises.explain: The e → ie change is kept: Lies!

exercises.prompt: Formal imperative of öffnen.
exercises.text: ___ Sie bitte das Fenster!
exercises.explain: Sie-imperative: verb first, then Sie.

exercises.prompt: Which is the du-imperative of sein?
exercises.text: ___ vorsichtig!
exercises.explain: sein is irregular: Sei! / Seid! / Seien Sie!

exercises.prompt: The pronoun does not belong in the du-imperative. Correct it.
exercises.text: Komm du bitte um acht!
exercises.explain: The du-imperative drops the pronoun.

topics.title: Suggestions with “Sollen / wollen wir …”, “Soll ich … ?” and “wir”
topics.summary: Sollen/Wollen wir …?, Soll ich …? and the wir-form as an invitation.

explanation.heading: Asking the other person
explanation.text: Sollen / Wollen wir …? proposes something and asks whether the other person wants it too. Soll ich …? offers your own help and asks whether that is wanted.

explanation.heading: The wir-form
explanation.text: A sentence starting with the wir-form of the verb, often with doch, is an invitation: Gehen wir doch ins Kino! means Ich schlage vor, wir gehen ins Kino.

rules: Sollen / Wollen wir …? = Ich schlage das vor. Möchtest du das auch?
Soll ich …? = Ich kann helfen. Möchtest du das?
Verb + wir + doch …! = Ich schlage vor, …
The particle doch makes the invitation friendlier.

examples.de: Sollen / wollen wir einen Kaffee trinken?
Soll ich helfen?
Gehen wir doch ins Kino!
Kochen wir doch mal zusammen!

exercises.prompt: You want to offer your help. Which is right?
exercises.explain: Soll ich …? offers your own help and asks whether it is wanted.

exercises.prompt: Turn the proposal into an invitation with the wir-form.
exercises.from: Sollen wir ins Kino gehen?
exercises.explain: Verb first, then wir, often with doch.

exercises.prompt: Complete the particle that softens the invitation.
exercises.text: Kochen wir ___ mal zusammen!
exercises.explain: doch makes the suggestion friendlier.

exercises.prompt: What does Sollen wir einen Kaffee trinken? mean?
options: Ich schlage das vor. Möchtest du das auch?
answers: Ich schlage das vor. Möchtest du das auch?
exercises.explain: It proposes something and asks whether the other person agrees.

topics.title: Subject position
topics.summary: The subject stands either first or straight after the verb — both are correct, so vary them.

explanation.heading: Two places
explanation.text: The subject is in the first position or after the verb. If something else opens the sentence — a time or a comment — the subject moves behind the verb, because the verb keeps position 2.

explanation.heading: Style
explanation.text: The document advises using both forms when writing, to get some variation.

rules: Subject first: Das Brunnenstüberl ist am Sonntag geöffnet.
Something else first, then verb, then subject: Am Sonntag ist das Brunnenstüberl geöffnet.
The conjugated verb stays in position 2 either way.
Use both forms when writing and make sure you have some variation.

examples.de: Am Sonntag ist das Brunnenstüberl geöffnet.
examples.note: time first, subject after the verb

examples.de: Das Brunnenstüberl ist am Sonntag geöffnet.
Das Wetter ist leider nicht so gut.
Leider ist das Wetter nicht so gut.
examples.note: adverb first, subject after the verb

exercises.prompt: Start the sentence with the time expression.
exercises.from: Das Brunnenstüberl ist am Sonntag geöffnet.
answers: Am Sonntag ist das Brunnenstüberl geöffnet.
exercises.explain: The verb stays in position 2, so the subject moves behind it.

exercises.prompt: Start the sentence with leider.
exercises.from: Das Wetter ist leider nicht so gut.
answers: Leider ist das Wetter nicht so gut.
exercises.explain: Whatever opens the sentence, the verb keeps position 2.

exercises.prompt: Which word order is correct?
options: Am Sonntag ist das Brunnenstüberl geöffnet.
Am Sonntag das Brunnenstüberl ist geöffnet.
Ist am Sonntag das Brunnenstüberl geöffnet.
Am Sonntag das Brunnenstüberl geöffnet ist.
answers: Am Sonntag ist das Brunnenstüberl geöffnet.
exercises.explain: The verb must be in position 2.

exercises.prompt: The verb has lost position 2. Correct the sentence.
exercises.text: Leider das Wetter ist nicht so gut.
answers: Leider ist das Wetter nicht so gut.
exercises.explain: After an opening adverb the verb comes next, then the subject.

topics.subsection: Position of a verb in a sentence
topics.source: DaF kompakt neu A1–B1 — Grammar explanations

topics.title: Word order for positive statements, W-questions and yes/no questions
topics.titleEn: Word order: statements, W-questions and yes/no questions
topics.summary: The verb is in position 2 in statements and W-questions, and in position 1 in yes/no questions.

explanation.heading: Position 2
explanation.text: In a statement and in a W-question the conjugated verb always stands in position 2. In a W-question position 1 is taken by the question word.

explanation.heading: Position 1
explanation.text: In a yes/no question there is no question word, so the verb itself moves to position 1.

rules: W-question: question word (Pos. 1) + verb (Pos. 2) — Woher kommen Sie?
Statement: subject or another element (Pos. 1) + verb (Pos. 2) — Ich komme aus Marokko.
Yes/no question: verb (Pos. 1) + subject — Kommen Sie aus Tunesien?

examples.de: Woher kommen Sie?
Ich komme aus Marokko.
Wo wohnst du?
Kommen Sie aus Tunesien?
Wohnst du in Stuttgart?

exercises.prompt: Make a W-question.
exercises.explain: Question word first, verb in position 2.

exercises.prompt: Make a yes/no question.
exercises.explain: In a yes/no question the verb takes position 1.

exercises.prompt: Where does the verb stand in a W-question?
exercises.explain: The question word takes position 1, the verb position 2.

exercises.prompt: This should be a yes/no question. Correct the word order.
exercises.text: Sie kommen aus Tunesien?
exercises.explain: A yes/no question puts the verb first.

topics.subsection: Position of a verb in a sentence
topics.source: DaF kompakt neu A1–B1 — Grammar explanations

topics.title: Word order for statements and W-questions
topics.summary: The modal verb takes position 2 and the main verb goes to the end as an infinitive.

explanation.heading: The verb bracket
explanation.text: With a modal verb the sentence has two verb parts: the conjugated modal verb in position 2 and the infinitive of the main verb at the very end. Everything else sits between them.

rules: Modal verb in position 2, infinitive at the end of the sentence.
In a W-question the question word takes position 1 and the modal verb position 2.
Separable verbs stay whole as the final infinitive: früh aufstehen.

examples.de: Beatriz muss in der Woche früh aufstehen.
Am Wochenende kann sie lange schlafen.
Man darf im Bus nicht laut Musik hören.
Beatriz und Leopold wollen heute ins Kino gehen.

explanation.heading: What changes
explanation.text: The agent is important in an active sentence — who is doing the action. In a passive sentence the action itself is important — what is being done. The accusative object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive one.

explanation.heading: Naming the agent
explanation.text: If it is important to mention the agent, this is done by adding von + dative. When man appears in the active sentence there is no agent in the passive sentence.

explanation.heading: Tenses
explanation.text: Present: werde/wirst/wird … + Partizip II. Preterite: wurde/wurdest/wurde … + Partizip II.

rules: Passive = werden + Partizip II, with the participle at the end of the sentence.
Active accusative object → passive subject.
The agent, when named, is added with von + Dativ.
man in the active = no agent in the passive.

topics.title: Second conditional: “haben”, “sein” “werden”“, “können”, “dürfen”, “müssen”, “sollen”, “möcht-“
topics.summary: hätte, wäre, würde, könnte, dürfte, müsste, möchte, sollte — and which take an umlaut.

explanation.heading: Built on the preterite
explanation.text: The second conditional is formed using the preterite. haben and werden, and the modal verbs können, dürfen and müssen, take an umlaut; sollen and wollen do not.

explanation.heading: What it is for
explanation.text: The second conditional expresses polite questions and requests, and also wishes and dreams about the future. They do not always have to be realistic.

explanation.heading: möchte
explanation.text: möcht- is the conditional form of mögen, but it replaces the modal verb wollen for polite requests and wishes in the present indicative.

rules: haben → hätte; sein → wäre; werden → würde.
können → könnte; dürfen → dürfte; müssen → müsste — all with an umlaut.
sollen → sollte and wollen have no umlaut in the second conditional.
Use it for polite questions, requests, wishes and dreams.

explanation.text: The ending -chen / -lein means something is small; -chen also means something is nice or attractive.

rules: -chen and -lein always make the noun neuter: das Röckchen, das Jäckchen.

explanation.text: In the dative the articles are dem (masculine), dem (neuter), der (feminine) and den (plural).

Akk.: den Sohn, das Kind, die Tochter, die Söhne.

Dative plural: wir → uns, ihr → euch, sie / Sie → ihnen / Ihnen.

explanation.heading: Article or pronoun
explanation.text: Before a noun mein is an article and may have no ending (mein Sohn). Used on its own, replacing the noun, it is a pronoun and always carries an ending.

explanation.heading: The ending copies the definite article
explanation.text: The document sets each definite article beside the pronoun it produces: der → meiner, das → meins, die → meine, dem → meinem, den → meinen.

explanation.heading: The one short form
explanation.text: das → meins is shortened; the other forms simply take the article's own ending.

Accusative: den → meinen (M); the N, F and plural forms are the same as in the nominative.
Dative: dem → meinem (M and N), der → meiner (F), den → meinen (plural).
The same endings apply to dein-, sein-, ihr-, unser-, euer- and Ihr-.

topics.title: “dies-”, “„der” / “das” / “die”
topics.titleEn: welch-, dies- and der / das / die as pointers
topics.summary: Ask with welch-, answer by pointing with dies- or with der / das / die.

explanation.heading: The question
explanation.text: welch- asks about things and people and takes the same endings as the definite article: welcher Pullover, welches Modell, welche Jacke.

explanation.heading: The answer
explanation.text: dies- and der / das / die point at the thing chosen. The document's answers are pairs — dieser / der, dieses / das, diese / die — where the second option is the plain definite article used as a pronoun.

explanation.heading: After a preposition
explanation.text: The preposition decides the case: zu takes the dative, so the question is zu welchem Pullover and the answer zu diesem / dem.

rules: welch- asks about things and people; dies- and der / das / die refer to them.
welch- and dies- carry the endings of the definite article.
Nominative and accusative are identical except in the masculine: welcher → welchen, dieser → diesen.
A preposition sets the case of the whole phrase.

explanation.heading: Two endings only
explanation.text: After der, das, die, den, dem the adjective ends in -e or -en — nothing else. The article has already shown the case and gender, so the adjective carries little work.

explanation.heading: Where -e appears
explanation.text: In the nominative of all three genders, and in the accusative of the neuter and the feminine: der lebendige Dialekt, das neue Leben, die lange Tradition.

Plural in every case: -en.

explanation.heading: The mixed pattern
explanation.text: ein, kein and mein behave like the definite article except in three boxes, where they have no ending of their own: nominative masculine, nominative neuter and accusative neuter.

explanation.heading: What the adjective does there
explanation.text: In exactly those three boxes the adjective takes the strong ending instead: ein neuer Trend, ein festliches Kleid, ein schwarzes Barett.

explanation.heading: The plural column
explanation.text: The table pairs the plural with an article-less form: schwarze Talare beside meine / keine männlichen Kollegen — ein- itself has no plural.

Nominative and accusative N: -es (ein festliches Kleid, ein schwarzes Barett).
Nominative and accusative F: -e (eine neue Phase, eine große Party).

topics.title: Adjectives before nouns without an article (=Nullartikel)
topics.summary: With no article the adjective takes over the article's own ending.

explanation.heading: The adjective stands in for the article
explanation.text: The table is written as a set of arrows — der → lebendiger Dialekt, das → neues Leben — because the ending the missing article would have had moves onto the adjective.

explanation.heading: How to work it out
explanation.text: Think of the definite article the phrase would take, strip the d-, and put what is left on the adjective: dem → -em, der → -er, den → -en.

explanation.heading: Where you meet it
explanation.text: Mass nouns and plurals without an article: neues Leben, lange Tradition, alte Lieder.

rules: Nominative: -er (M), -es (N), -e (F), -e (plural).
Accusative: -en (M); the neuter, feminine and plural endings are unchanged.
Dative: -em (M and N), -er (F), -en (plural).
In the dative plural the noun still adds -n: alten Liedern.

topics.title: Comparative sentences

explanation.heading: Equal, or not equal
explanation.text: For etwas / jemand ist gleich / nicht gleich use the basic form with so … wie: genauso gern … wie, nicht so attraktiv wie.

explanation.text: For etwas / jemand ist mehr use the comparative with als: billiger als, gesünder als, mehr Sportmöglichkeiten als.

explanation.heading: The regular pattern
explanation.text: Add -er for the comparative and am …sten for the superlative: attraktiv, attraktiver, am attraktivsten.

explanation.heading: When -esten appears
explanation.text: Adjectives ending in -t, -d, -s, -ß or -z insert an e in the superlative: bekannt → am bekanntesten, alt → am ältesten.

explanation.heading: Umlaut
explanation.text: Several short adjectives take an umlaut in both forms: groß → größer → am größten, alt → älter → am ältesten, hoch → höher → am höchsten.

explanation.text: gut → besser → am besten; gern → lieber → am liebsten; viel → mehr → am meisten; hoch → höher → am höchsten; teuer loses its second e: teurer.

explanation.heading: The nine
explanation.text: an, auf, in, über, unter, hinter, vor, neben, zwischen can take either case; the case is chosen by the question, not by the preposition.

explanation.heading: Wohin? → accusative
explanation.text: Movement towards a goal: Stell den Kaffee ins Regal! The contractions are an das → ans, auf das → aufs, in das → ins, and colloquially hinters, übers, unters, vors.

explanation.heading: A quick test
explanation.text: If the verb is stellen, legen, setzen, hängen (put) the case is accusative; with stehen, liegen, sitzen, hängen (be) it is dative.

rules: Wohin? → accusative. Wo? → dative.

topics.title: Expressing reasons: Causal connectives “darum”, “deshalb”, “deswegen”, “daher”
topics.summary: The same reason stated the other way round, with the consequence as a main clause.

explanation.heading: Reason first, consequence second
explanation.text: A weil clause names the reason; darum, deshalb, deswegen and daher turn the sentence round so that the reason comes first as a main clause and the consequence follows.

explanation.heading: Position 1
explanation.text: The connector fills position 1 of the second main clause, so the conjugated verb comes second and the subject third: … darum gehe ich jeden zweiten Tag walken.

explanation.heading: Four words, one meaning
explanation.text: The document lists darum, deshalb and deswegen as interchangeable in both examples, with daher in the heading.

rules: darum, deshalb, deswegen, daher introduce the consequence, not the reason.
They occupy position 1, so the verb comes second and the subject follows it.
Weil ich Sport machen soll, … becomes Ich soll Sport machen, darum …
The clause they open is a main clause, so the verb does not move to the end.

topics.group: VI. Compound sentences and statements within a sentence
topics.title: Time expressions: dependent clauses with “seit(dem)” [• →] and “bis” [• → •]
topics.summary: seit(dem) marks a starting point that still holds; bis marks an end point.

explanation.heading: seit(dem)
explanation.text: The clause names the moment something started, and the situation has lasted since: Beate hat dauernd Schmerzen, seit(dem) sie an ihrer Masterarbeit arbeitet. The document marks this with the symbol • →.

explanation.heading: bis
explanation.text: The clause names the moment something will stop or stopped: Es dauert noch 2 Wochen, bis Beate zu Dr. Rosmann gehen kann. The document marks it • → •, an interval with both ends.

explanation.heading: Both orders
explanation.text: Each conjunction is shown after and before the main clause. A leading subordinate clause is position 1, so the main clause begins with its verb: Seit(dem) Beate so viel arbeitet, hat sie dauernd Schmerzen.

explanation.heading: Tenses
explanation.text: The examples pair present with present (arbeitet – hat) and past with past (bekam – dauerte).

rules: seit(dem) names the starting point of a situation that still holds.
bis names the end point of a period.
Both are subordinating conjunctions: the verb goes to the end.
Either clause can come first; a leading subordinate clause fills position 1.
seitdem and seit are both possible in this use.

examples.de: Beate hat dauernd Schmerzen, seit(dem) sie an ihrer Masterarbeit arbeitet.

Seit(dem) Beate so viel arbeitet, hat sie dauernd Schmerzen.
Bis Beate zu Dr. Rosmann gehen kann, dauert es noch 2 Wochen.

exercises.explain: The document marks it with • →, an open-ended stretch.

topics.group: VI. Compound sentences and statements within a sentence
topics.title: Indirect questions
topics.summary: ob for yes/no questions, the question word otherwise — and the verb at the end.

explanation.heading: Yes/no questions take ob
explanation.text: If the direct question is a yes/no question, the indirect question begins with ob: Gibt es auch Führungen …? → Ich möchte wissen, ob es auch Führungen … gibt.

explanation.heading: W-questions keep their word
explanation.text: If the direct question begins with a question word, the indirect question will begin with the same question word: wie lange, wo, welches.

explanation.heading: The verb moves to the end
explanation.text: In every example the conjugated verb closes the clause: gibt, dauert, ist, ist.

explanation.heading: Why use it
explanation.text: The introductory phrases — Ich möchte wissen, Können Sie mir sagen, Können Sie mir zeigen — make the question more polite.

rules: Yes/no question → ob.
W-question → the same question word.
The conjugated verb goes to the end of the indirect question.
The introduction is a main clause and keeps its own word order.
A comma separates the introduction from the indirect question.

examples.de: Gibt es auch Führungen zum Thema „Film“?
Ich möchte wissen, ob es auch Führungen zum Thema „Film“ gibt.
examples.note: ob, with gibt at the end

examples.de: Können Sie mir sagen, wie lange die Führung dauert?
Können Sie mir auf dem Plan zeigen, wo der Treffpunkt ist?
examples.note: wo, with ist at the end

examples.de: Ich möchte gern wissen, welches Ticket am besten ist.
examples.note: welches, with ist at the end

exercises.explain: ob is the indirect counterpart of a question with no question word.

topics.group: VI. Compound sentences and statements within a sentence
topics.title: Relative clauses and relative pronouns
topics.summary: Gender and number come from the noun; the case comes from the relative clause.

explanation.heading: The forms
explanation.text: The table is almost the definite article: Nom. der, das, die, die; Akk. den, das, die, die; Dat. dem, dem, der, denen. Only the dative plural denen differs.

explanation.heading: Where gender comes from
explanation.text: The gender (der, die, das) and whether the pronoun is singular or plural depends on the noun which the relative pronoun is referring to: Ich hatte einen Berater, der sehr kompetent war.

explanation.heading: Where case comes from
explanation.text: The case depends either on the verb in the relative clause (treffen + accusative) or on the preposition (hören von + dative) — not on the main clause.

explanation.heading: Position
explanation.text: Relative clauses are dependent clauses, so the verb goes to the end, and the clause often begins directly after the word it is referring to.

rules: Gender and number come from the noun in the main clause.
Case comes from the verb or the preposition inside the relative clause.
The forms match the definite article except in the dative plural: denen.
The conjugated verb stands at the end of the relative clause.
The relative clause often follows its noun immediately.

examples.de: Ich hatte einen Berater, der sehr kompetent war.
examples.note: der Berater is masculine; the pronoun is the subject of the relative clause, so nominative

examples.de: Nom. der das die die
examples.note: the nominative row of the table

examples.de: Akk. den den die die
examples.note: the accusative row as printed in the document

examples.de: Dat. dem dem der denen
examples.note: the dative row — denen is the one form that differs from the article

exercises.explain: der Berater, and the pronoun is the subject — nominative masculine.

answers: Ich hatte einen Berater, der sehr kompetent war.

topics.group: VI. Compound sentences and statements within a sentence
topics.title: Temporal subordinate clauses with “wenn” and “als”
topics.summary: als for one past occasion, wenn for a repeated one — and for everything present or future.

explanation.heading: als — once, in the past
explanation.text: als is used for an action that happened once in the past: Als wir dort waren, hat eine Musikgruppe traditionelle Musik gespielt.

explanation.heading: wenn — repeatedly, in the past
explanation.text: wenn is used for a repeated action in the past, often with immer or jedes Mal in front of it: (Immer) wenn das Wetter gut war, haben wir Wanderungen in den Bergen gemacht.

explanation.heading: wenn — present and future
explanation.text: For a single or a repeated action in the present or the future the conjunction is always wenn: Man erholt sich am besten, wenn man faulenzt.

explanation.heading: The optional dann
explanation.text: When the wenn clause comes first, the main clause may add dann before the verb: Wenn das Wetter morgen schön ist, (dann) machen wir einen Ausflug.

rules: Past, once: als.
Past, repeated: wenn — often with (immer) or (jedes Mal).
Present or future, single or repeated: wenn.
Both send the conjugated verb to the end of their clause.
A leading wenn or als clause fills position 1, so the main clause starts with the verb; dann may be inserted.

examples.de: Das Wetter war leider nicht so gut, als wir ankamen
examples.note: als — one occasion in the past

examples.de: Als wir dort waren, hat eine Musikgruppe traditionelle Musik gespielt.
(Immer) wenn das Wetter gut war, haben wir Wanderungen in den Bergen gemacht.
(Jedes Mal) wenn wir sehr müde waren, haben wir einen Pausentag eingeplant.
Man erholt sich am besten, wenn man faulenzt.
Wenn das Wetter morgen schön ist, (dann) machen wir einen Ausflug.
examples.note: wenn in the future, with the optional dann

exercises.explain: als marks one past occasion.

exercises.explain: als is restricted to the past.

topics.title: Time expressions usually go in the middle field before expressions of place.
topics.titleEn: Time before place in the middle field
topics.summary: In the Mittelfeld, when comes before where.

explanation.heading: The middle field
explanation.text: The document's columns are Position 1, Position 2, Mittelfeld and Satzende. Everything between the conjugated verb and the closing verb form is the middle field.

explanation.heading: The rule
explanation.text: Time expressions usually go in the middle field before expressions of place: diese Woche schon fünfmal im Kino, nach dem Frühstück sofort ins Museum.

explanation.heading: The sentence bracket
explanation.text: In the first two examples the participle closes the sentence — gewesen, gegangen — which is what creates the middle field. The third example has no second verb, so the middle field simply follows waren.

rules: Time comes before place in the middle field.
The conjugated verb stays in position 2 and any second verb form closes the sentence.
Everything between them is the middle field.

topics.title: Modal verbs in the perfect
topics.summary: haben + the second verb's infinitive + the modal verb's infinitive at the very end.

explanation.heading: The double infinitive
explanation.text: Modal verbs in the perfect tense are formed with haben plus the infinitive of the modal verb. The modal verb is placed at the end of the sentence, after the infinitive form of the second verb.

rules: haben + Infinitiv (main verb) + Infinitiv (modal verb).
The modal verb comes last, not the main verb.
There is no participle: it is arbeiten müssen, never gemusst.

examples.de: In der ersten Zeit in Dresden hat Christian viel arbeiten müssen .
Er hat daher das Schloss noch nicht besuchen können .

answers: Er hat das Schloss nicht besuchen können.

topics.title: Past perfect for active verbs
topics.summary: hatte/war in the preterite + past participle, for what happened before something else in the past.

explanation.heading: What it is for
explanation.text: The past perfect expresses an action in the past which happened before something else in the past.

explanation.heading: How it is formed
explanation.text: haben or sein in the preterite plus the past participle — hatte geschafft, war herumgelaufen.

explanation.heading: Where it appears
explanation.text: It is used in the subordinate clause with nachdem; the main clause then contains verbs in the preterite or the perfect.

rules: hatte / war (preterite) + Partizip II.
The choice of hatte or war follows the same rule as the perfect.
nachdem + past perfect in the subordinate clause, preterite or perfect in the main clause.
The two clauses never both use the past perfect.

examples.de: Nachdem wir es bis zum Bahnhof Zoo geschafft hatten , fing es an zu regnen.
examples.note: past perfect in the nachdem-clause, preterite in the main clause

examples.de: Nachdem wir ein bisschen herumgelaufen waren , haben wir dort gegessen .
examples.note: war-form, then the perfect in the main clause

exercises.explain: A movement verb takes sein, here in the preterite: waren.

topics.title: Future I
topics.summary: werden + infinitive for intentions and predictions; particles shift it between assumption and certainty.

explanation.heading: Form and use
explanation.text: The simple future tense is used to express intentions and predictions where the outcome is certain. It is formed using werden in the present tense and the infinitive, which goes to the end of the sentence.

explanation.heading: Particles change the meaning
explanation.text: Adverbs and particles decide whether Futur I reads as an assumption, an assurance or a certainty.

rules: werden in position 2, infinitive at the end of the sentence.
Assumption: vermutlich, wohl, wahrscheinlich.
Assurance: schon.
Certainty: bestimmt, sicherlich, sicher.
The particle may also stand in position 1, with werden still in position 2.

examples.de: Zur Vorbereitung werde ich einen Schwedischkurs machen.
Wir werden ab August zusammen in Berlin wohnen.
Ich werde vermutlich / wohl / wahrscheinlich Portugal vermissen.
Es wird schon klappen.
Ich werde als Dolmetscher bestimmt / sicherlich / sicher gute Chancen haben.

exercises.explain: werden in position 2, infinitive at the end.

answers: Wir werden ab August zusammen in Berlin wohnen.
exercises.explain: werden in position 2, the infinitive last.

topics.title: “(sich) lassen” + Verb
topics.summary: lassen with a second infinitive, and where lassen goes in the perfect or with a modal verb.

explanation.heading: lassen plus an infinitive
explanation.text: The verb (sich) lassen is often used with the infinitive of a second verb — you have something done, or you let something happen.

explanation.heading: In the perfect
explanation.text: The perfect of lassen + verb is formed with haben plus lassen in the infinitive, not as a participle.

explanation.heading: Word order
explanation.text: In sentences in the perfect tense or with modal verbs, lassen goes after the infinitive of the second verb.

rules: lassen + Infinitiv of the second verb.
Perfect: haben + Infinitiv + lassen (not gelassen).
With a modal verb: modal verb in position 2, then the second infinitive, then lassen.

examples.de: Christian lässt sich in der Informatikabteilung das Passwort vom Computer geben .
Christian hat sich schon das Intranet zeigen lassen .
Christian muss den Urlaubsantrag der Personalabteilung zukommen lassen .

exercises.text: Christian hat sich schon das Intranet ___.
exercises.explain: The perfect uses haben + infinitive + lassen, never gelassen.

answers: Christian hat sich schon das Intranet zeigen lassen.
Christian hat sich das Intranet zeigen lassen.
exercises.explain: haben + zeigen + lassen.

exercises.prompt: Complete the word order with a modal verb.
exercises.text: Christian muss den Urlaubsantrag der Personalabteilung zukommen ___.
exercises.explain: lassen comes after the infinitive of the second verb.

exercises.text: Christian hat sich das Passwort geben gelassen.
answers: Christian hat sich das Passwort geben lassen.

topics.title: “lassen” + Nouns
topics.summary: With a noun or pronoun, lassen means to leave something — and then it does take a participle.

explanation.heading: A different lassen
explanation.text: The verb lassen can also be used with a noun or a pronoun rather than a second verb. It then means to leave something somewhere.

explanation.heading: The perfect
explanation.text: The perfect of lassen + noun is formed with haben and the past participle of lassen — gelassen, not the infinitive.

rules: lassen + noun or pronoun = to leave something somewhere.
Perfect: haben + gelassen (the ordinary participle).
Contrast with lassen + verb, which keeps the infinitive lassen in the perfect.

examples.de: Christian lässt sein Handy im Büro.
Christian lässt es im Büro.
Christian hat sein Handy im Büro gelassen .

exercises.prompt: lassen + noun in the perfect — which form?
exercises.text: Christian hat sein Handy im Büro ___.

exercises.text: Christian hat sein Handy im Büro lassen.
answers: Christian hat sein Handy im Büro gelassen.
exercises.explain: With a noun the perfect is gelassen.

topics.title: “brauchen zu” + infinitive
topics.summary: brauchen nur zu = you only have to; brauchen nicht/kein … zu = you don't have to.

explanation.heading: Only that and nothing more
explanation.text: brauchen … nur zu + infinitive expresses that you don't need to do anything else but that.

explanation.heading: Not necessary
explanation.text: brauchen … nicht zu and brauchen … kein … zu + infinitive have the same meaning as nicht müssen.

rules: brauchen … nur zu + Infinitiv = you only have to do that.
brauchen … nicht zu + Infinitiv = nicht müssen.
brauchen … kein … zu + Infinitiv = also nicht müssen.
The zu stands directly before the infinitive at the end of the sentence.

examples.de: Sie brauchen nur die Broschüre „Länderinformationsschrift Österreich“ zu bestellen .
examples.note: nur zu — nothing else is needed

examples.de: Sie brauchen nicht lange zu warten .
Sie brauchen keine weiteren Informationen im Internet zu suchen .

exercises.from: Sie müssen nicht lange warten.
answers: Sie brauchen nicht lange zu warten.
exercises.explain: nicht müssen = brauchen … nicht zu + infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Complete the particle before the infinitive.
exercises.text: Sie brauchen nicht lange ___ warten.
exercises.explain: brauchen takes zu before the infinitive.

exercises.prompt: What does brauchen … nur zu express?
options: You don't need to do anything else but that.
You are not allowed to do it.
answers: You don't need to do anything else but that.
exercises.explain: nur zu limits what is required to that one thing.

exercises.prompt: brauchen needs zu here. Correct the sentence.
exercises.text: Sie brauchen nicht lange warten.
answers: Sie brauchen nicht lange zu warten.
exercises.explain: In this construction brauchen is followed by zu + infinitive.

topics.title: Past perfect – Passive
topics.summary: war + Partizip II + worden, for a passive action completed before another past event.

explanation.heading: How it is formed

topics.title: Second conditional
topics.summary: When to use a real Konjunktiv II form and when to fall back on würde + infinitive.

explanation.heading: Why würde exists
explanation.text: For regular verbs the form of the second conditional is the same as the preterite, so it would be ambiguous. For this reason we use würde + infinitive instead.

explanation.heading: Verbs that keep a real form
explanation.text: The second conditional is used with haben, sein, the modal verbs and certain frequently used irregular and mixed verbs. Otherwise use würde + infinitive.

rules: Regular verbs: würde + Infinitiv — er schaute nach → er würde nachschauen.
haben, können, müssen, dürfen and mixed verbs like wissen: preterite + umlaut — ich hatte → ich hätte, du konntest → du könntest, er wusste → er wüsste.
Irregular verbs: preterite + ending -e + umlaut — ich kam → ich käme, du warst → du wärest, sie fand → sie fände, er ging → er ginge.
In practice, use a real form for haben, sein, the modals and common irregular verbs; use würde for everything else.

topics.title: Reference to something identical: demonstrative pronouns and articles „derselbe“, „dasselbe“, „dieselbe“
topics.titleEn: derselbe, dasselbe, dieselbe — the very same one
topics.summary: A two-part word: der- carries the case, -selb- takes the adjective ending.

explanation.heading: What it means
explanation.text: derselbe, dasselbe, dieselbe describe a thing or a person identical to one mentioned earlier or later — not merely a similar one.

explanation.heading: Two parts, two jobs
explanation.text: The first part (der- / das- / die-) follows the article and case of the noun; the second part (-selb-) takes the same ending an adjective would take after a definite article.

explanation.heading: The pattern to remember
explanation.text: der große Platz → derselbe Platz. Wherever the adjective would end in -e, so does -selb-.

rules: It works as both a demonstrative pronoun and a demonstrative article.
Part one is declined like the definite article: der-, das-, die-, den-, dem-.
Part two takes the weak adjective ending: -selbe, -selben, -selbem, -selber.
The two parts are written as one word.

topics.title: Indefinite pronouns and adverbs with “irgend-”
topics.summary: A prefix that stresses that it does not matter which one.

explanation.heading: What it adds
explanation.text: irgend- reinforces the fact that it is not important which one — English any at all.

explanation.heading: Three hosts
explanation.text: It attaches to question words (wann, wie, wo), to the indefinite article ein, and to indefinite pronouns (jemand, wer / wen / wem, etwas).

explanation.heading: The colloquial pair
explanation.text: irgendetwas has the everyday form irgendwas, built on the spoken was.

irgend- + indefinite article: ein → irgendein.
irgend- + indefinite pronoun: jemand → irgendjemand; wer / wen / wem → irgendwer / irgendwen / irgendwem.
etwas → irgendetwas, colloquially irgendwas.
irgendein and irgendwer keep the endings of the word they are built on.

topics.title: Question word “wo(r)...? ” , prepositional pronouns “da(r...) ”
topics.summary: Ask about a thing with wofür, worin, worauf; refer back to it with dafür, darin, darauf.

explanation.heading: Asking about a thing
explanation.text: A question built on was plus a preposition becomes one word beginning wo-, or wor- before a vowel: für was → wofür, in was → worin.

explanation.heading: Asking about a person
explanation.text: People keep the preposition and the pronoun apart: wer, wen, wem with the preposition in front — Auf wen freut sich Bernd?

explanation.heading: Referring back
explanation.text: The prepositional pronoun da(r)- refers to a noun, or even to a whole sentence, through a preposition: Darin stehen wenig Möbel = in dem Zimmer.

explanation.heading: Backwards and forwards
explanation.text: It can point back to something already said (anaphora) or forward to what comes next (cataphora) — Frau Egger kann sich darauf verlassen, dass Bernd drei Monate bleibt.

rules: Questions with was + preposition become wo(r)-: für was → wofür, in was → worin.
The r appears before a vowel: worin, worauf, worüber; but wofür, womit, wovon.
da(r)- works the same way for statements: darin, darüber, darauf.
da(r)- can refer back (anaphora) or forward (cataphora), typically to a dass-clause.
For people use wer / wen / wem with the preposition kept separate.

explanation.heading: Two or more people, the same action
explanation.text: When two or more people do the same thing to one another, the reflexive pronoun means each other — einander, gegenseitig — rather than oneself.

explanation.heading: Which subjects
explanation.text: Use man for singular subjects, and all the plural subjects wir, ihr, sie / Sie.

explanation.heading: Separable verbs keep their prefix at the end

rules: The reciprocal sense can be spelled out with einander or gegenseitig.
man + sich, wir + uns, ihr + euch, sie / Sie + sich.

The reflexive pronoun is the same word as in the ordinary reflexive use; only the meaning differs.

topics.title: Relative pronouns “was” / “wo(r)-”
topics.summary: The relative pronoun for a whole clause or for words like alles, nichts, etwas.

explanation.heading: When was is the relative pronoun
explanation.text: was refers to a whole sentence, or to a pronoun such as das, nichts, alles, etwas, einiges, vieles — not to an ordinary noun, which takes der / das / die.

explanation.heading: With a preposition
explanation.text: was does not contract with a preposition. Use wo(r)- plus the preposition instead: wofür, worauf, worüber, womit.

explanation.heading: Where the preposition comes from
explanation.text: The document shows the verb behind each form: einverstanden sein mit → womit; aufmerksam machen auf → worauf.

rules: was refers back to a whole clause or to das, nichts, alles, etwas, einiges, vieles.
A preposition never combines with was; use wo(r)- + preposition.
The r is inserted before a vowel: worauf, worüber — but wofür, womit.
Which preposition appears is decided by the verb of the relative clause.

topics.title: Comparisons: comparative and superlative – attributive
topics.titleEn: Comparative and superlative before a noun
topics.summary: The comparative and superlative keep the ordinary adjective endings.

explanation.heading: Two endings stacked
explanation.text: Before a noun the adjective carries the comparison marker first and the declension ending second: höher + e → höhere, höchst + e → höchste.

explanation.heading: Nothing new to learn
explanation.text: The document states it as a rule: adjectives have the same basic endings when they are in the comparative or superlative form.

explanation.heading: No am here
explanation.text: The predicative superlative am höchsten becomes der höchste Berg before a noun — the article replaces am.

explanation.heading: The one restriction
explanation.text: It is not possible to have a superlative before a noun with the indefinite article, which is why the table's ein- row jumps straight from ein höherer Berg to kein / sein höchster Berg.

rules: The comparison ending comes first, the declension ending second: der höher-e Berg, der höchst-e Berg.
The endings are exactly those of the basic form.
The predicative am …sten is replaced by an article plus the declined superlative.
A superlative cannot stand after ein-; kein- and the possessive articles are fine.

topics.title: Giving reasons: causal connectives
topics.summary: A preposition with the genitive, and an adverb that never starts the sentence.

explanation.text: wegen names the reason as a noun phrase in the genitive: Wegen der Kombination aus Theorie und Praxis …

explanation.heading: nämlich is not a conjunction
explanation.text: nämlich is a connecting adverb. It stands inside the second sentence, after the conjugated verb — never in first position and never before it.

explanation.heading: What it does
explanation.text: The sentence with nämlich supplies the reason for the sentence before it: Ich muss ein Auslandssemester machen. Ich habe nämlich vor, …

rules: wegen takes the genitive and can open the sentence.
nämlich is a connecting adverb, placed after the conjugated verb in the middle field.
nämlich cannot stand in first position.

topics.summary: Two-part connectors that replace und, emphasise, or negate both halves.

explanation.heading: Replacing und
explanation.text: nicht nur … sondern auch and sowohl … als auch both replace the conjunction und.

explanation.heading: Equal weight
explanation.text: sowohl … als auch expresses that the listed elements are equally important: Innsbruck bietet sowohl Kultur als auch Natur.

explanation.text: With nicht nur … sondern auch the second element is emphasised more strongly: nicht nur die Architektur, sondern auch die Aussicht.

explanation.heading: Neither
explanation.text: weder … noch means that neither element is applicable. It is negative in itself, so no nicht is added — and after noch the verb may come first, as in the document's example: … noch ist die Speisekarte aufregend.

sowohl … als auch: the elements are equally important.
nicht nur … sondern auch: the second element carries the emphasis.
weder … noch: neither element applies; no further negation is used.

explanation.heading: What it says
explanation.text: Improbable conditional sentences in the second conditional use wenn to express a condition in the dependent clause which has not been fulfilled, so the result will not — or possibly will — be fulfilled in the future.

explanation.heading: Reading the example
explanation.text: Wenn Markus den Paketschein hätte, könnte er nachforschen … means the opposite is true: Markus hat den Paketschein nicht, daher kann er nicht nachforschen.

explanation.text: The Konjunktiv II appears in both clauses: hätte … könnte, wäre … könnte.

topics.title: simultaneity
topics.summary: One clause at the same time as another, or one after the other.

explanation.heading: At the same time
explanation.text: Subordinate clauses with während are used to express two things happening at the same time.

explanation.heading: One after the other
explanation.text: Subordinate clauses with bevor and nachdem are used to express two things which happen one after the other — nachdem for what came first, bevor for what came second.

explanation.heading: Tense with nachdem
explanation.text: The document's example pairs Plusquamperfekt in the nachdem clause with a simple past main clause: Nachdem wir es bis zum Bahnhof Zoo geschafft hatten, fing es an zu regnen.

explanation.heading: A note on the heading
explanation.text: This block's heading runs on from the previous page, where it reads: Temporal subordinate clauses with nachdem, bevor, während – anteriority, posteriority and … simultaneity.

rules: während: the two events overlap in time.
nachdem: the subordinate clause happens first, the main clause afterwards.
bevor: the subordinate clause happens second.

With nachdem the earlier clause usually stands one tense further back (Plusquamperfekt with a past main clause).

topics.summary: A reason that exists but does not take effect.

explanation.heading: What concessive means here
explanation.text: Concessive connectors indicate an invalid counter-argument: there is a reason not to do something, or that something will not happen, but it is not effective — the person does it, or it happens anyway.

explanation.heading: How the document builds it
explanation.text: It starts from a plain reason — Lateinkenntnisse sind hilfreich, and that is why the Latinum used to be compulsory — and then turns that same reason into the counter-argument.

explanation.heading: obwohl
explanation.text: The connector obwohl introduces a subordinate clause, so its verb goes to the end: Obwohl Lateinkenntnisse im Studium sehr hilfreich sein können, …

explanation.heading: Either order
explanation.text: The obwohl clause may come first or second; the counter-argument is in the subordinate clause either way.

rules: obwohl introduces the counter-argument as a subordinate clause.
The conjugated verb goes to the end of the obwohl clause.
The obwohl clause can precede or follow the main clause.
A leading obwohl clause fills position 1, so the main clause begins with its verb.
Unlike trotzdem and dennoch, which are main-clause connectors, obwohl is a conjunction.

examples.de: Lateinkenntnisse können im Studium sehr hilfreich sein. Deshalb war das „Latinum“ früher fast immer Pflicht.
examples.note: the plain reason, before it becomes the counter-argument

examples.de: Obwohl Lateinkenntnisse im Studium sehr hilfreich sein können, ist das „Latinum“ heute nur noch selten Pflicht.
examples.note: obwohl clause first — the main clause opens with ist

examples.de: Das „Latinum“ ist heute nur noch selten Pflicht, obwohl Lateinkenntnisse im Studium sehr hilfreich sein können.
examples.note: the same content with the obwohl clause second

topics.group: VI. Compound sentences and statements within a sentence
topics.title: Infinitive phrases
topics.summary: zu + infinitive at the end of the sentence, after expressions like Lust haben or vorhaben.

explanation.heading: The basic shape
explanation.text: Infinitive phrases are formed with zu + infinitive, and both go at the end of the sentence: Irina hätte Lust, das Hafenfest zu besuchen.

explanation.heading: What comes before them
explanation.text: They often follow expressions such as Lust haben, vorhaben, es gut / schlecht / … finden, es lieben, and Es ist … + adjective.

explanation.heading: Separable verbs
explanation.text: For verbs with a separable prefix, zu goes between the prefix and the stem of the verb: mitfahren → mitzufahren, printed in the document as mit zu fahren.

explanation.heading: Passive
explanation.text: In passive sentences, zu goes between the past participle and werden: angerempelt zu werden.

rules: zu + infinitive stands at the end of the phrase.
Common triggers: Lust haben, vorhaben, es gut finden, es lieben, Es ist + adjective.
Separable verbs put zu between the prefix and the stem: mitzufahren.
Passive infinitives are past participle + zu + werden.
A comma separates the infinitive phrase from the main clause.

examples.de: Irina hätte Lust, das Hafenfest zu besuchen.
Eleni findet es gut, ins Theater zu gehen.
Irinas Bruder hat vor, ins Musical zu gehen.
Antonia liebt es, auf einem Schiff mit zu fahren.
examples.note: separable verb — the document prints the split to show where zu goes

examples.de: Es ist am schlimmsten, angerempelt zu werden.

exercises.prompt: Put the sentence in order.
answers: Irinas Bruder hat vor, ins Musical zu gehen
exercises.explain: The separable prefix vor closes the main clause; the infinitive phrase follows the comma.

exercises.prompt: Which expression does NOT usually introduce an infinitive phrase here?
exercises.explain: weil introduces a subordinate clause with a conjugated verb, not a zu-infinitive.

topics.group: VI. Compound sentences and statements within a sentence
topics.title: Naming the aim: Final dependent clauses and statements (wozu?)
topics.titleEn: Purpose: damit, um … zu, zum / zur / für
topics.summary: Saying what something is for — wozu?

explanation.heading: damit for two different subjects
explanation.text: damit is used when the subject is different in the main and subordinate clause: Man sollte sich … melden, damit diese ihre zukünftigen Helfer vorher kennen lernen.

explanation.heading: um … zu for the same subject
explanation.text: When the subject is the same in both halves, the usual form is um … zu + infinitive: Man arbeitet als WWOOFer, um praktische Erfahrung im Bio-Landbau zu sammeln.

explanation.heading: Either half first
explanation.text: Both structures can open the sentence, in which case the main clause begins with its verb: Damit die Landwirte …, sollte man …; Um praktische Erfahrung … zu sammeln, arbeitet man …

explanation.heading: Without a clause at all
explanation.text: The purpose can also be a noun phrase with zum, zur or für, usually referring to an action: für die Mithilfe, zum Geldverdienen.

rules: Different subjects → damit + subordinate clause, verb at the end.
Same subject → um … zu + infinitive at the end.
Either structure may stand before the main clause.
zum / zur / für + noun states the purpose without a clause.
The question this answers is wozu?

topics.group: VI. Compound sentences and statements within a sentence
topics.title: Stating consequences: consecutive sentences – “sodass” / “so … dass”, “folglich”, “also”
topics.summary: A consequence in a subordinate clause, with the connector optionally split.

explanation.heading: sodass
explanation.text: Consequences can be expressed in the subordinate clause with sodass, whose verb goes to the end: …, sodass man manchmal einfach nur müde ist …

explanation.heading: Splitting it
explanation.text: The subordinate connector sodass can be separated. This puts so in the main clause with an adjective or an adverb, and the subordinate clause begins with dass: Es ist so anstrengend …, dass man …

explanation.heading: The difference from also and folglich
explanation.text: sodass builds a subordinate clause; also and folglich are main-clause connectors. The document shows the same content in both forms.

rules: sodass introduces the consequence as a subordinate clause: verb at the end.
sodass can be split into so (in the main clause) + dass (opening the subordinate clause).
When split, so stands directly before the adjective or adverb it intensifies.
A comma precedes sodass and dass.

examples.de: Es ist anstrengend mehrere Stunden am Tag eine Fremdsprache zu lernen, sodass man manchmal einfach nur müde ist und dann leichter Fehler macht.
Es ist so anstrengend mehrere Stunden am Tag eine Fremdsprache zu lernen, dass man manchmal einfach nur müde ist und dann leichter Fehler macht.
examples.note: split: so with the adjective, dass opening the clause

exercises.explain: so joins the adjective in the main clause and dass opens the subordinate clause.

at the end of the main clause
answers: in the main clause, before the adjective or adverb

exercises.explain: Unlike also and folglich, sodass sends the verb to the end.

answers: Es ist anstrengend, sodass man manchmal müde ist.
exercises.explain: In a sodass clause the conjugated verb comes last.

topics.title: Zustandspassiv (sein + Partizip II)
topics.summary: sein + Partizip II describes the result; werden + Partizip II describes the action.

explanation.heading: Two passives, two questions
explanation.text: The werden-passive answers what is being done: Die Tür wird geöffnet — somebody is opening it right now. The sein-passive answers what state something is in afterwards: Die Tür ist geöffnet — it is open.

explanation.heading: How it is built
explanation.text: sein in the tense you need, plus the Partizip II, with no worden. The moment worden appears you are in the werden-passive again: Das Haus ist gebaut worden is the action, Das Haus ist gebaut is the state.

explanation.heading: Why B1 needs it
explanation.text: It is mostly a recognition skill at this level — you meet it constantly in signs and instructions (Geschlossen, Reserviert) and need to hear that it reports a condition, not an event.

explanation.heading: The test that always works
explanation.text: If you can add gerade (right now) the sentence is a werden-passive; if you can add immer noch (still) it is a Zustandspassiv.

rules: Zustandspassiv = sein + Partizip II. Vorgangspassiv = werden + Partizip II.
The Zustandspassiv names a result or condition; the werden-passive names an action in progress.
There is no worden in a Zustandspassiv — worden belongs to the werden-passive perfect.
Past tense: Die Tür war geöffnet (state) against Die Tür wurde geöffnet (action).
Only verbs that describe a change of state form a useful Zustandspassiv: öffnen, schließen, reparieren, lösen.

examples.de: Die Tür ist geöffnet.
Die Tür wird geöffnet.
Das Problem ist gelöst.
Das Auto ist repariert.
Das Haus ist gebaut worden.
Das Haus wird gebaut.

topics.title: Verben mit fester Präposition
topics.summary: Many verbs demand one particular preposition, and that preposition fixes the case.

explanation.heading: The preposition is part of the verb
explanation.text: warten auf, träumen von, sich freuen auf — the preposition is not chosen by meaning, it is learned with the verb. English does the same thing (to wait FOR, to dream OF) and rarely picks the same one, which is why it has to be memorised rather than translated.

explanation.heading: The preposition sets the case
explanation.text: The list writes the case after the preposition: A for accusative, D for dative. warten auf A means auf takes the accusative here — Ich warte auf den Bus — even though auf is a two-way preposition.

explanation.heading: Asking about one
explanation.text: For a thing, the question word is wo(r)- plus the preposition: Worauf wartest du? For a person, the preposition stays separate: Auf wen wartest du? That is the same split covered under wo(r)- and da(r)-.

explanation.heading: Two prepositions at once
explanation.text: A few verbs take two: sich entschuldigen bei D für A — you apologise to somebody for something.

explanation.heading: One entry to distrust
explanation.text: The list prints glauben an D. That is an error in the source: glauben an takes the accusative — Ich glaube an dich, not *an dir. It is shown here as printed, with this warning, rather than quietly corrected.

rules: The preposition belongs to the verb and must be learned with it.
The preposition fixes the case, even for two-way prepositions: warten auf + Akkusativ.
A marks the accusative and D the dative in the list below.
Ask about a thing with wo(r)- + preposition, about a person with the preposition + wen/wem.
Some verbs govern two prepositional objects: sich entschuldigen bei jemandem für etwas.

topics.title: Subjektive Bedeutung der Modalverben
topics.titleEn: Subjective meaning of the modal verbs
topics.summary: müssen, dürfen and können express how certain the speaker is; sollen and wollen report a claim.

explanation.heading: Objective and subjective meaning
explanation.text: Modal verbs have a subjective meaning alongside their objective one. In the present tense only the context tells you which of the two is meant; in the past the two are told apart by their different forms.

explanation.heading: Degrees of certainty
explanation.text: müssen, dürfen and können say how sure the speaker is about the statement: muss = absolutely sure (100 %), müsste = almost sure (90 %), dürfte = probable (75 %), könnte = possible (50 %).

explanation.heading: Reporting a claim
explanation.text: sollen and wollen express claims. sollen reports someone else's claim; wollen reports a claim the speaker has made about themselves.

rules: muss = the speaker is sure it is so, but has no proof and has not checked it.
müsste = the speaker supposes it.
dürfte = the speaker thinks it probable.
könnte = the speaker thinks it possible; the uncertainty is relatively high.
sollen = it is reported by others, e.g. in the media.
wollen = the person claims it about themselves.
For the past, the modal verb is followed by the Infinitiv Perfekt: muss ... gehandelt haben, soll ... geschwommen sein.

examples.de: Es muss sich um eine Sucht handeln.
examples.note: 100 % — the speaker is sure, but has no proof.

Er müsste den Zug eigentlich noch bekommen, da er glücklicherweise Verspätung hat.
Die Sucht dürfte besonders junge Leute betreffen.
Die Nervosität könnte von der Handysucht kommen.
Der Täter soll sich zurzeit im Ausland aufhalten.
Eine 56-Jährige will durch den Ärmelkanal geschwommen sein.
examples.note: wollen — she claims it about herself.

exercises.explain: muss = the speaker is sure, but has no proof.

answers: Der Täter soll sich zurzeit im Ausland aufhalten.
exercises.explain: sollen reports someone else's claim; wollen would be the man's own claim.

exercises.prompt: Order the four by certainty: which is the least certain?
exercises.explain: muss 100 % > müsste 90 % > dürfte 75 % > könnte 50 %.

topics.title: Wortbildung: Vorsilben miss-, zer-, ent- und de-
topics.titleEn: Word formation: the prefixes miss-, zer-, ent- and de-
topics.summary: Four inseparable prefixes that give the base verb a different, often negative meaning.

explanation.heading: What they do
explanation.text: The inseparable prefixes miss-, zer-, ent- and de- give the base verb a different, frequently negative meaning.

explanation.heading: Verbs already carrying ge-
explanation.text: If the base verb has the prefix ge-, that prefix drops and is replaced by miss-, e.g. gelingen – misslingen.

rules: miss- reverses or negates the base verb: gefallen → missfallen, trauen → misstrauen.
zer- expresses destruction or something going to pieces: reden → zerreden, laufen → zerlaufen.
ent- expresses removal or taking away: kleiden → entkleiden, sorgen → entsorgen.
de- reverses a technical or formal process, mostly with Latinate verbs: installieren → deinstallieren, stabilisieren → destabilisieren.
All four prefixes are inseparable and unstressed; the Partizip II has no ge-: missfallen, zerredet, entsorgt, deinstalliert.

examples.de: Max misstraut den Berichten über solche Rekordversuche.
Man sollte die Glücksmomente aber nicht zerreden.
Dem Modell ist das Make-up total zerlaufen.
Bei manchen beginnt die Entspannung bereits, wenn sie sich entkleiden.
Plastikabfall wurde in speziellen Containern entsorgt.
Ein Kollege hilft mir, das alte Programm auf dem Computer zu deinstallieren.
Durch das viele Laufen wurden die Wirbel wieder leicht destabilisiert.

exercises.explain: miss- negates the base verb: trauen → misstrauen.

exercises.prompt: Complete the verb of disposal.

exercises.explain: ent- expresses removal: sorgen → entsorgen.

exercises.explain: With base verbs carrying ge-, that prefix drops and is replaced by miss-: gelingen – misslingen.

exercises.prompt: Which prefix undoes a technical process such as installieren?
exercises.explain: de- reverses a technical or formal process: installieren → deinstallieren.

answers: Dem Modell ist das Make-up total zerlaufen.
exercises.explain: zer- expresses that something goes to pieces.

answers: Ein Kollege hat das alte Programm deinstalliert.
exercises.explain: miss-, zer-, ent- and de- are inseparable and unstressed, so the Partizip II takes no ge-.
